summary: Best verified state 5553e312219ab670: 1.492x over the baseline (240 pairs, CI 1.491-1.493; 0.178 ms against 0.266 ms), just under the 1.5x target, entirely at machine level on the baseline's own code (no source state of mine is in its ancestry). Against amdclang's code it (1) reads the two wave-uniform query rows with s_load_dwordx16 into SGPRs and uses them as scalar operands of v_fmac, where amdclang issued 8 per-lane global_load_dwordx4 of identical addresses per iteration (2/3 of the key loop's vector loads); (2) keeps 16 key loads in flight per wait (9 iterations of 256 B per lane instead of 36 of 64 B); (3) in the value loop issues all 16 row loads up front into their final registers and selects the probability with op_sel on v_pk_fma, where amdclang waited after every pair of loads and shuffled with ~60 v_mov per iteration. Which case this is: not at the memory floor in the model's sense (headroom 7.3) because the kernel re-reads the KV cache once per workgroup - about 1.2 GB of key reads and 1.07 GB of value reads against 20 MB of tensors; the key phase (about 103 us of 178 us, estimated from probes) now moves that at roughly 11.7 TB/s, so further gain needs fewer re-reads, not a faster loop. Caveat: the per-phase split comes from probes of other states (key loop cut to one iteration), not from a direct measurement of this state.

friction: liveness(id, block) reports every VGPR/SGPR as live in and live out of every block (e.g. .LBB0_7 of baseline lists v0-v124 and s0-s67), so it cannot answer 'which registers are dead across this loop'. I had to infer free registers from what amdclang's own loop overwrote, and that inference was wrong once: state 456f50a21daa83a5 (24 loads into v66-69, v86-101, v114-125) fails the battery, most likely a clobbered live register. A real per-block liveness, or a static_check finding 'this edit writes a register that is read later without redefinition', would have caught it before a GPU run.

edit() ops address the parent's listing, so replacing a whole block means delete(index 1, count N-1) + replace(index 0) with the exact block length; an off-by-one (count 95 vs 94 in state 3da5999365ad4de3 .LBB0_7) refused the edit and forced resending a 320-line text. A 'replace_block' op, or a count that may run to the end of the block, would avoid it.
The edit result echoes the full ops text back; with 300-line loop bodies that doubles the size of every exchange.

No way to generate repetitive IR: the 16- and 24-load key loops are 32 near-identical v_fmac lines per chunk written out by hand (up to 240 lines). A repeat/template facility in edit text (loop over a register list) would make batching sweeps (8/16/24 loads) cheap and less error-prone.

SGPRs are the binding resource for the scalar-query lever: 32 scalars per 64 B chunk for 2 heads, only s68-s101 free, x16 loads must start on a multiple of 4 and s102+ is unusable, so 4 heads needed x16 + 2 x8 into clobbered constants (s60-s67) with rematerialization in .Lft3. A tool listing SGPRs that are dead across a given loop (constants only used elsewhere) would have saved the manual find() passes.
find() with \b around bracketed tuples silently misses them (pattern '\bs\[30:31\]\b' matched nothing); I had to search tuples separately to confirm s[30:31] and s[14:15] were constant.

probe() cannot remove a phase safely when a fallback loop exists: masking off the unrolled value loop (state 3c97954d0bacb386) just routed the work to the tail loop. A per-block time attribution would give the phase split directly; the split I report for the best state is extrapolated from probes of other states.

bench's traffic/headroom model (20 MB, headroom 7-11) is far from this kernel's real traffic (about 2.3 GB re-read from cache across 256 workgroups); I had to work the real numbers out by hand to decide the lever.
lessons: Wave-uniform rows loaded per lane are a large machine-level win when amdclang does it: in mla_decode 8 of 12 vector loads per key-loop iteration were the two query rows at identical addresses for all 64 lanes. Replacing them by 2x s_load_dwordx16 and v_fmac_f32_e64 acc, sN, vK gave 1.27x alone (0.266 -> 0.210 ms), bit-order kept.

After that, loads in flight in the key loop paid again: 4 -> 16 global_load_dwordx4 per wait gave 0.202 -> 0.178 ms on the 2-head build (1.32x -> 1.49x) and 0.217 -> 0.196 ms on the 4-head build, with one serial scalar reload (lgkmcnt(0)) per 64 B chunk in between. Per-iteration time before batching was about 1.8 us for 4 loads regardless of wave count (4096 or 2048 waves), i.e. latency-like, not bandwidth.

amdclang's interleaved (vectorize-by-2) value loop issues loads two at a time with a full wait after each pair and ~60 v_mov shuffles; issuing all 16 up front with op_sel-selected operands (no moves) gave only +4% (1.27 -> 1.32x), and the row-at-a-time tail loop ran the same phase within 4%: that phase reads 1 KB contiguous per wave from cache and is not latency-bound.

v_pk_fma_f32 with op_sel:[0,1,0] / op_sel_hi:[1,0,1] broadcasts one half of a ds_read2_b64 pair to both lanes of the packed op, so (p_h0, p_h1) read as one 64-bit LDS value serves two heads with no v_mov; ds_read2_b64 offsets (8-bit, units of 8 B) reach 2 KB from one base register.

More heads per workgroup did not beat 2 heads here even with scalar queries: HB=4 (128 workgroups) reached 1.36x against 1.49x for HB=2 (256 workgroups). Key time dropped only 103 -> 90 us for half the key bytes while the rest grew 75 -> 106 us (estimates from probes). Consistent with the note 'pick the count so workgroups about equal the 256 CUs'. amdclang's own HB=4 build is 0.81x of its HB=2 build.

SGPR budget for scalar operands: s68-s101 are typically free (34), x16 loads need a start on a multiple of 4, so two x16 sets fit (s[68:83], s[84:99]); beyond that, loop-external constants can be clobbered inside a loop and rematerialized with s_mov in the loop's exit block (done for s60-s67, passes the battery).

Do not assume a register is dead across a loop because another loop of the kernel overwrites it: using v66-69, v86-101, v114-125 as extra load targets in the key loop broke the battery (state 456f50a21daa83a5), while the subset the original loop itself wrote plus v70-v85 was fine. liveness() does not distinguish these today.

session.final:
The best verified state is `5553e312219ab670` at **1.492x** over the baseline (0.178 ms against 0.266 ms; 240 pairs, CI 1.491–1.493), just short of the 1.5x target. It passes the static check and the full battery (98/98), and it is a pure machine-level gain on the baseline's own code.

What it does differently from amdclang:

1. **Scalar query rows.** amdclang loaded the two query rows per lane, at the same address for all 64 lanes; that was 8 of the 12 vector loads in each key-loop iteration. They are now two `s_load_dwordx16` into SGPRs, used as scalar operands of `v_fmac`. This alone gave 1.27x.
2. **16 key loads in flight per wait.** The key loop runs 9 iterations of 256 B per lane instead of 36 of 64 B. This took it from 1.32x to 1.49x.
3. **Value loop without per-pair waits.** All 16 row loads are issued up front into their final registers, and the probability is selected with `op_sel` on `v_pk_fma`, removing about 60 `v_mov` per iteration. This added only about 4%.

| State | Change | Result |
|---|---|---|
| `3f02231e49857562` | scalar query rows | 1.27x |
| `89b2fb3c055eb3b9` | + value loop rewrite | 1.32x |
| `5553e312219ab670` | + 16 key loads in flight | **1.49x** |
| `456f50a21daa83a5` | + 24 key loads in flight | fails the battery, never timed |
| `c400c01c4cf49d68` | source with 4 heads per workgroup, as amdclang builds it | 0.81x |
| `320413cb1361d3bd` | 4 heads + scalar queries + 16 in flight | 1.36x |

- **The failed state:** the 24-in-flight variant produced wrong `out` and `lse` on the first battery case. I did not diagnose it; the likely cause is that one of the extra registers I used as load targets is live across the key loop.
- **Which case this is:** not the memory floor in the model's sense (headroom 7.3). The kernel re-reads the KV cache once per workgroup, about 2.3 GB of cached reads against 20 MB of tensors. The key phase is roughly 103 of the 178 µs, extrapolated from probes of other states rather than measured on this one. Further gai
